lessonTitle: Infant Feeding, Severe Acute Malnutrition and Immunisation

blocks.text: A nursery sends home a letter: one child has measles and the room contains three babies too young for their first dose. Whether those babies stay healthy depends on what fraction of everyone around them is immune, and on what those babies are fed, how they are protected and how they are treated if they are malnourished. This lesson links three prevention tools: feeding, nutritional rescue and vaccination.

blocks.markdown:
## Infant feeding

**Breast milk** is the reference food for infants: it provides energy and nutrients in the right balance, **secretory IgA, lactoferrin and other immune factors**, and reduces the risk of gastrointestinal and respiratory infection and of necrotising enterocolitis in preterm babies. UK and WHO guidance advise **exclusive breastfeeding for about the first 6 months**, with continued breastfeeding alongside solid food, as long as mother and baby wish. Breastfed infants should receive a daily vitamin D supplement, and all newborns are offered vitamin K at birth to prevent haemorrhagic disease of the newborn.

**Formula feeding.** When breast milk is not used, a first infant formula based on cow's milk is appropriate. A guide is about **150 mL per kg per day** after the first week, divided into feeds every 3 to 4 hours. Do not use cow's milk as the main drink before 12 months because of its low iron and high solute load.

**Complementary feeding** begins at about **6 months** (not before 17 weeks), when the infant can sit with support, hold the head steady, and has lost the tongue-thrust reflex. Reasons: energy and iron needs outstrip what milk alone can supply, and the gut and swallowing are ready. Start with iron-rich foods (meat, pulses, fortified cereal), progress through textures (puree to finger food), introduce common allergenic foods (egg, peanut, in suitable form) rather than avoiding them, offer water in a cup, and avoid **added salt and sugar** and **honey before 12 months** (risk of infant botulism, because the infant gut flora cannot resist *Clostridium botulinum* spores).

blocks.caption: A guide to formula volume after the first week; individual babies vary and feeding to appetite is encouraged.

blocks.title: Formula volume per feed
blocks.prompt: A 3.4 kg infant is exclusively formula fed with 7 feeds a day. Use 150 mL per kg per day to estimate the volume per feed.

steps.text: Daily volume: weight times 150 mL per kg.
Divide by the number of feeds.
Interpret: this is a guide; the baby should be offered feeds responsively and weight gain monitored, adjusting volume as the infant grows.

blocks.answer: The daily volume is 510 mL, about 73 mL per feed.

blocks.markdown:
## Severe acute malnutrition (SAM)

Worldwide, malnutrition remains a major cause of child death. **SAM** in a child aged 6 to 59 months is defined by any of: **weight-for-height z-score below -3**, **mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) below 115 mm**, or **bilateral pitting oedema** (kwashiorkor). **Moderate acute malnutrition** has weight-for-height z-score between -3 and -2 or MUAC 115 to under 125 mm. **Marasmus** is severe wasting without oedema; **kwashiorkor** shows oedema, skin and hair changes, and a fatty liver, and the oedema alone means SAM.

The key distinction for management is **complicated versus uncomplicated** SAM. *Uncomplicated* SAM (good appetite, alert, clinically well) is treated at home with **ready-to-use therapeutic food (RUTF)** and a short course of oral antibiotics, with regular follow-up. *Complicated* SAM (poor appetite, vomiting, oedema, infection, hypoglycaemia, hypothermia, lethargy, severe dehydration) requires **inpatient care**.

Inpatient treatment follows WHO phases. In stabilisation: treat or prevent **hypoglycaemia** (feed early, give glucose), **hypothermia** (keep warm), **dehydration** (use low-sodium ORS for malnutrition, *ReSoMal*, orally or by nasogastric tube, and avoid IV fluids except in shock because the heart is fragile and sodium overload is risky), correct **electrolyte** imbalance (low potassium and magnesium), treat **infection** with broad-spectrum antibiotics even if there are no signs, give **micronutrients** (vitamin A, folate, zinc; iron only after recovery begins), and start **cautious feeding** with a low-osmolarity, low-protein milk (F-75) at about 130 mL per kg per day. In rehabilitation, move to energy-dense F-100 or RUTF for catch-up growth, with sensory stimulation and discharge planning. Over-rapid refeeding causes refeeding syndrome with electrolyte shifts.

blocks.title: Classifying malnutrition
blocks.prompt: A 20-month-old boy has a weight-for-height z-score of -3.4, no oedema, an MUAC of 112 mm, is alert, afebrile and finishes a test portion of RUTF. How would you classify and manage him?

steps.text: Check the criteria: a weight-for-height z-score below -3 and an MUAC below 115 mm each meet the definition of SAM. There is no oedema, so this is marasmic-type SAM.
Check for complications: he is alert, has no fever and passes the appetite test, so there are no signs of complicated SAM.

Decide the setting: uncomplicated SAM is managed as an outpatient with RUTF and a short course of antibiotics according to protocol, with weekly review of weight and MUAC, plus screening for HIV and tuberculosis and addressing the household cause.

blocks.answer: Uncomplicated severe acute malnutrition, treated at home with RUTF, oral antibiotics and close follow-up; admission is needed if complications or loss of appetite develop.

blocks.markdown:
## Immunisation: principles

Vaccines train the adaptive immune system without causing disease. **Inactivated, toxoid and conjugate vaccines** (such as diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, polio injection, Hib, hepatitis B, pneumococcal, meningococcal) need multiple doses and boosters. **Live attenuated vaccines** (MMR, BCG, rotavirus, nasal influenza, varicella) give stronger, longer immunity from fewer doses but are **avoided in significant immunosuppression and in pregnancy**.

**Schedules** are timed to the window in which maternal antibody has waned and the infant can respond, and to the age at which disease is most dangerous: in the UK, primary doses start at 8 weeks, then continue at later intervals, followed by boosters and a second measles-containing dose. Exact schedules differ between countries and change over time, so use the current national schedule (summarised in the table below). Premature infants are immunised by **chronological age**, not corrected age.

**Contraindications.** True contraindications are few: a **severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis)** to a previous dose or a vaccine component; and **live vaccines in children who are significantly immunosuppressed** (for example on chemotherapy or high-dose steroids). **Not** contraindications: mild illness without systemic upset (cold, low-grade fever), a family history of adverse reactions, prematurity, asthma or eczema, antibiotic therapy, breastfeeding, and, for MMR, egg allergy. A child with a moderate or severe acute illness is vaccinated after recovery. When two live vaccines are not given on the same day, leave at least 4 weeks between them.

blocks.caption: Herd immunity threshold: the minimum proportion of the population that must be immune to stop sustained spread of an infection with basic reproduction number R0 (the average number of people an infectious person infects in a fully susceptible population).

blocks.title: Herd immunity threshold
blocks.prompt: An infection has a basic reproduction number R0 of 5. What proportion of the population needs to be immune to prevent sustained spread, assuming a perfect vaccine and random mixing?

steps.text: Write the threshold formula and substitute R0 equal to 5.
Calculate: 1 divided by 5 is 0.2, so the threshold is 0.8.

Interpret: each infected person then infects on average fewer than one other. A real vaccine is imperfect and mixing is not random, so coverage targets are set higher (for measles, above 95% of children with two doses).

blocks.answer: 80% of the population must be immune; higher coverage is needed in practice because vaccines are imperfect.

blocks.title: Immunise on time and know the real contraindications
blocks.text: Delay or omission of vaccines because of a mild cold, prematurity, asthma or egg allergy is a common error. True contraindications are anaphylaxis to a previous dose or component, and live vaccines in the significantly immunosuppressed. Premature babies are vaccinated at their chronological age.

points: Exclusive breastfeeding is advised for about 6 months; complementary foods start at about 6 months with iron-rich foods, avoiding honey before 12 months and added salt and sugar; formula volume is about 150 mL per kg per day.
SAM is defined by weight-for-height below -3 z, MUAC below 115 mm, or bilateral pitting oedema; uncomplicated cases are treated at home with RUTF and complicated cases as inpatients.
Inpatient SAM care addresses hypoglycaemia, hypothermia, dehydration (ReSoMal, avoid IV unless shock), electrolytes, infection and micronutrients before cautious feeding (F-75) and catch-up feeding.
Vaccines are live attenuated or inactivated; the herd immunity threshold is 1 minus 1 over R0.
True contraindications are anaphylaxis to a previous dose or component and live vaccines in significant immunosuppression; mild illness and prematurity are not.

questions.stem: According to UK and WHO guidance, until what age is exclusive breastfeeding recommended for a healthy term infant?

distractorRationale.a: Exclusive breastfeeding is advised for about the first 6 months, then continued alongside solid food.
distractorRationale.b: Two months is far too early to add other foods.
distractorRationale.c: By 9 months complementary food should already be established.
distractorRationale.d: Breastfeeding may continue beyond 12 months but not exclusively.

questions.explanation: At about 6 months energy and iron needs exceed what milk alone can provide and the infant is developmentally ready for solids. Breastfeeding continues alongside complementary feeding for as long as mother and baby wish.

questions.stem: A mother of a 9-month-old asks what she should avoid giving. Which item should be avoided because of the risk of infant botulism?

distractorRationale.a: Honey may contain Clostridium botulinum spores, which can colonise the infant gut before 12 months.
distractorRationale.b: Banana is a safe complementary food.
distractorRationale.c: Egg is suitable and early introduction of allergenic foods is encouraged.
distractorRationale.d: Fortified cereal helps meet iron needs.

questions.explanation: The infant gut flora is not yet able to suppress Clostridium botulinum spores, so honey is avoided before 12 months. Other foods listed are appropriate, and delaying egg is no longer advised.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old has a mid-upper arm circumference of 118 mm, no oedema, is alert and eating well. How is this classified?

distractorRationale.a: A MUAC of 115 to under 125 mm without oedema is moderate acute malnutrition.
distractorRationale.b: Severe acute malnutrition needs MUAC below 115 mm, a z-score below -3 or oedema.
distractorRationale.d: MUAC below 125 mm in this age group indicates malnutrition.

questions.explanation: A MUAC of 118 mm lies in the 115 to under 125 mm band that defines moderate acute malnutrition. It is below the normal range but above the 115 mm threshold for severe disease, and the child needs nutritional support and monitoring.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old with bilateral pitting oedema, lethargy, a temperature of 35.0 degrees Celsius and a blood glucose of 2.0 mmol per litre is admitted. Which statement about management is correct?

options.text: Treat hypoglycaemia and hypothermia, give broad-spectrum antibiotics, and use cautious feeding with F-75; avoid IV fluids unless in shock
Give a large IV saline bolus to correct the oedema
Start high-protein feeds immediately for rapid catch-up
Give a high dose of iron on admission

questions.correctOptionText: Treat hypoglycaemia and hypothermia, give broad-spectrum antibiotics, and use cautious feeding with F-75; avoid IV fluids unless in shock

distractorRationale.a: This follows the stabilisation phase: correct hypoglycaemia and hypothermia, treat presumed infection and feed cautiously.
distractorRationale.b: The malnourished heart is fragile and total body sodium is raised; saline loading risks heart failure.
distractorRationale.c: Over-rapid refeeding with protein overloads function and risks refeeding syndrome.
distractorRationale.d: Iron is withheld until recovery has started because it can worsen infection.

questions.explanation: Oedema, lethargy, hypothermia and hypoglycaemia mean complicated SAM requiring stabilisation. The priorities are glucose, warmth and antibiotics, with careful low-volume feeding because fluid or nutrient overload in malnutrition can be fatal.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a true contraindication to giving a vaccine?

options.text: Anaphylaxis to a previous dose of the same vaccine

questions.correctOptionText: Anaphylaxis to a previous dose of the same vaccine

distractorRationale.a: A severe allergic reaction to a previous dose or component is a true contraindication.
distractorRationale.b: Mild illness without systemic upset is not a reason to delay.
distractorRationale.c: Premature infants are immunised by chronological age.

questions.explanation: Anaphylaxis to a previous dose or a vaccine component is one of the few absolute contraindications, along with live vaccines in significant immunosuppression. A mild cold, prematurity and eczema are common false contraindications that cause unnecessary delay.

questions.stem: A mother asks you about starting solid food for her 6-month-old breastfed baby. Describe the principles of complementary feeding and the foods or practices to avoid.
markingGuide: Start at about 6 months (not before 17 weeks) when the infant sits with support, holds the head steady and has lost the tongue-thrust reflex
Reason: energy and iron needs exceed what milk alone can provide
Continue breastfeeding alongside solids
Offer iron-rich foods such as meat, pulses and fortified cereals
Progress textures from puree to lumpy and finger foods; offer water from a cup
Introduce allergenic foods such as egg and peanut in appropriate form rather than avoiding them
Avoid honey before 12 months, added salt and sugar, and cow's milk as the main drink before 12 months
Give a vitamin D supplement to breastfed infants and avoid choking hazards
questions.explanation: Complementary feeding at about 6 months supplements milk with iron and energy as the infant becomes developmentally ready. Safe practice avoids honey, added salt and sugar and cow's milk as a main drink, and uses suitable textures to avoid choking.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old with kwashiorkor is admitted to hospital with oedema, a poor appetite and diarrhoea. Outline the key steps of inpatient management of complicated severe acute malnutrition, giving the reasoning behind the treatment of dehydration and the use of iron.
markingGuide: Complicated SAM requires inpatient care (poor appetite, oedema, infection)
Stabilisation: treat or prevent hypoglycaemia and hypothermia
Dehydration: use ReSoMal orally or by nasogastric tube; avoid IV fluids unless in shock because of cardiac fragility and sodium overload
Correct electrolyte imbalance (potassium, magnesium); do not give diuretics for oedema
Give broad-spectrum antibiotics routinely
Micronutrients (vitamin A, folate, zinc); iron only after recovery begins because it may worsen infection
Cautious feeding with F-75 initially, then rehabilitation with F-100 or RUTF for catch-up growth
Sensory stimulation, screening for HIV and tuberculosis, and discharge planning and follow-up
questions.explanation: Inpatient SAM care is staged: life-threatening problems are stabilised first and nutrition is rebuilt cautiously. IV fluids are avoided unless in shock because the malnourished heart and kidney handle fluid and sodium poorly, and iron is delayed because free iron promotes bacterial growth.

questions.stem: Explain the difference between live and inactivated vaccines, give two examples of each, and state the contraindications and false contraindications to immunisation. How should a baby born at 29 weeks' gestation be immunised?
markingGuide: Live attenuated: weakened organism replicates, strong immunity from few doses (examples MMR, BCG, rotavirus, nasal influenza)
Inactivated, toxoid or conjugate: need several doses and boosters (examples tetanus, Hib, hepatitis B, pneumococcal, meningococcal)
True contraindications: anaphylaxis to a previous dose or component; live vaccines in significant immunosuppression or pregnancy
False contraindications: mild illness, family history, prematurity, asthma or eczema, antibiotics, breastfeeding
Moderate or severe acute illness: defer until recovery
Leave at least 4 weeks between live vaccines if not given on the same day
Premature babies are immunised by chronological age, on time, not corrected age
questions.explanation: Live vaccines replicate and mimic natural infection, so they are unsafe in significant immunosuppression, whereas inactivated vaccines cannot cause the disease. Premature infants have the same disease risk (or higher) so vaccinations start at the normal chronological age.

questions.stem: A 4.2 kg formula-fed infant is to be offered milk at 150 mL per kg per day. Calculate the total daily volume in mL.
questions.explanation: The daily volume is 4.2 kg multiplied by 150 mL per kg, which is 630 mL per day. This is a guide only, and feeding is adjusted according to hunger cues and weight gain.

questions.stem: A vaccine-preventable infection has a basic reproduction number R0 of 6. Assuming a perfect vaccine and random mixing, calculate the herd immunity threshold as a percentage of the population.
questions.explanation: The threshold is 1 minus 1 divided by R0, which is 1 minus 1/6, equal to 0.833 or 83.3%. Because real vaccines are not perfect and mixing is not random, coverage targets must be higher than this theoretical value.
